I wanted to be able to block subverses from /v/all without visiting them. So I whipped up a little javascript that seems to do the job for me. I'm using Personalized Web to run it on all voat.co/v/all URLs in Chrome. I also added a little CSS to style my added links. This is totally optional, and totally customizable.

I haven't looked at the source of VES, but it should be possible to add this as a feature. Feel free to offer suggestions or improvements. It works, but it its a pretty quick-and-dirty hack right now.

Usage: it will add a "[BLOCK]" link just to the right of subverse names under the link title. Clicking gives you an undo link and 5 seconds to change your mind. After the time's up, the link (and any other from the same subverse) will disappear. From then on, it's the same as if you had blocked it normally.

javascript:

timeouts = [];
 
function block(s, t) { 
 clearTimeout(timeouts[s]);
 $.ajax({
 type:'POST',
 url:'/subverses/block/'+s
 })
 .done(
 function(r){
 if(r=='Subverse block request was successful.') {
 if(t.innerHTML == '[BLOCK]') {
 timeouts[s] = setTimeout(function() { hide(s); }, 5000);
 }
 $(t).animate({opacity:0}, 400, function(){
 t.innerHTML = (t.innerHTML == '[BLOCK]' ? '[UNDO]' : '[BLOCK]');
 $(t).animate({opacity:1}, 400);
 });
 }
 }
 );
}
 
function hide(s) {
 $('.subverse').each(
 function(){
 if(this.innerHTML == s) {
 $(this).closest('.submission').hide(600);
 }
 }
 );
}
 
window.onload = function() {
 $('.subverse').each(
 function(){
 $(this).after(' <a class="block" href="javascript:void(0)" onclick="block(\''+this.innerHTML+'\', this)">[BLOCK]</a>');
 }
 );
};

CSS:

.block {
 color: darkred !important;
 font-size: 0.8em;
}

I'll give my thoughts from a slightly different perspective.

When I started browsing the web, there was no google. We started by getting URLs from printed magazines. Also, as kids, we weren't allowed on the internet all day, so we had to hurry, do what we came for, and leave. It trained us to use it as any other tool - with an agency in mind. You never just browsed for the sake of browsing, never just checked because you were bored, you did it because you had an intent to do something.

Now fast forward to the "streams", always on culture, and everywhere access via smartphone. Suddenly, the internet wants something from you, and not the other way around. It's easy to lose the intent, to come here without something specific in mind and be enticed by the carefully crafted presentation. And at the core of it, that's exactly what the article laments. New generations of web users, that don't really use the web. They use just an app. A node on the web, but never the web itself.

The comparison to TV is very apt. It's the same kind of plop down, switch off brain, no intent required, kind of instant entertainment. Don't even need to touch the remote to make a decision. The stream just goes on and on. I can see how that is appealing to a lot of people today. Some are mentally worn out after work, others were just raised that way and have problems formulating intents - easy fodder for the spoon-feeding of the streams.

If you read all that and then arrived here, in the comments: congratulations. You're not part of the problem. You have just demonstrated agency. Now go out and teach others what that means...

Sidenote: I shortly pondered if voat was also a kind of stream, where you just scroll through, without deeper interest. But it kinda isn't. You have to set up all the subserves, search them out, and subscribe. It's more like a group organized feed reader.
